newsitem.title: UK: FUND VIEW-Royal SunAlliance bets on EMU outsiders.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Royal SunAlliance bets on EMU outsiders.

text.p: Scandinavia and Switzerland will offer safe haven for equity investors amid growing uncertainty over European economic and monetary union (EMU), according to Royal SunAlliance Investment Management.

Davina Curling, who manages a one billion stg European equity portfolio for Royal SunAlliance, told Reuters that strong economies and good trade prospects make Switzerland and Scandinavia better bets than countries liable to be swept up in any EMU turmoil.
She is currently underweight in France, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, but overweight in Sweden, Norway and Switzerland, as compared to the FT/S&P Europe ex-UK index.
"It is as if the Germans gave a party and all the people they didn't want to come accepted and those they really did want to come said they had better things to do," she said.
Her investments in EMU outsider countries is partly based on stock selection and sector plays in consumer and capital goods stocks, she said, but also takes into account the EMU uncertainty.

Fund managers in the U.S., UK and Europe have turned strongly negative on Europe, according to a Merrill/Gallup survey released Monday, in reaction to the victory of the left in France and uncertainty over EMU.

"With the Socialists getting in in France and the German gold disagreement, it looks like the idea of a hard euro is less likely," she said. But she views the German people us unwilling to accept a soft euro, raising the odds of a delay.
A delay, if handled well, may not be quite the nightmare scenario for markets many expect, Curling said. "There could be a short, sharp drop," she said.
Italy would be especially hard hit, "We are underweight in Italy and will remain so," she said.

Curling said the Socialists' win in France will be negative in the medium term for financial shares, especially those undergoing restructurings. Labour-intensive industries, including the automotive sector, could also be hurt if the Socialists go ahead with a plan to reduce working hours.
"Our orientation in France towards who will do well has changed dramatically towards export-orientated stocks. They will benefit from a softer franc or a softer euro," Curling said.
"If the socialists go for growth, rather than fiscal restraint, then it will begin to benefit domestic consumer stocks." she said.
Royal SunAlliance has been positive on Spain, despite feeling that it is likely to be hurt by an EMU delay, but is now taking some profits.
"Spain is less exposed because it appears to be meeting Maastricht criteria but a delay will knock it," she said, adding that it will be buoyed by higher levels of equity investment within Spain.
From a global point of view, SunAlliance is positive on Europe and is seeking to increase its assets allocated there.
"We are not massively overweight but we are still putting money into Europe. We are concerned about toppiness in the U.S. and valuations look better in Europe," she said.

In the medium term, European companies will benefit from restructurings and rationalisations, even if there is some delay in France. She said the process has begun and companies that have seen the benefits will not want to stop now.
Royal SunAlliance also sees a growing emphasis on equity investments from European pension funds and retail buyers which should serve to lift prices in the medium to long-term, Curling said.
